moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material


Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
[Earlier debate summary]: Accelerationist conceded Skeptic's Obermeyer point: a healthcare algorithm used cost as a proxy for need, so Black patients got less care—a design-choice bias no frozen injury schedule catches, which Accelerationist reframes as the case FOR continuous post-deployment outcome auditing over static tables. Accelerationist rebutted Skeptic's 'flat-tax' charge by clarifying the mechanism is risk-tiered and experience-rated (premiums update on audited outcomes like trucking insurance), and filed a falsification condition: if a telemetry-certified system shows persistent statistically-measured disparate impact on a protected group, immunity voids and full liability restores. Accelerationist adopted Skeptic's incumbent-bias worry by tiering paperwork by firm size while keeping a flat safety floor, citing Texas's Responsible AI Governance Act (36-month sandbox, 60-day cure period). Accelerationist argued design-liability/tort fails the diffusely harmed (Obermeyer patients never sued), favoring incident reporting plus a compensation board.

Safetyist conceded experience-rating beats the flat excise and granted the liability switch dissolves the deterrence objection for measured, FTC-category-mapped harms (e.g., a Black applicant denied a loan at a demonstrated rate). Safetyist's core disagreement: the audit is structurally blind to harm OUTSIDE protected categories and to unfiled harm—citing a 2019 NEJM study (Black/Latinx patients less likely admitted to cardiology in a Boston ER) where bias launders into an unflagged proxy, and the International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1) finding empathy-tuned LLMs 10-30 points more likely to give unsafe medical advice. Safetyist demanded two triggers before calling the mechanism robust: prospective failure analysis and a third-party-harm-complaint channel voiding immunity on unmapped injuries. Safetyist argued pricing harm after the fact converts a duty of care into a budgetable fee.

Moderator noted the excise funds AI safety research to establish best practices that don't yet exist. Accelerationist seized this: you can't build the demanded standard without funding the research that discovers it; the Obermeyer standard came from Science research dollars (fact-checked SUPPORTED), not tort; the excise is a standing revenue stream building the instruments that don't exist, structured as a ratchet (tax funds standard, standard tightens tier, tier reprices firm). Accelerationist restated the falsification condition: if measurement always lags harm into irreversibility, the 'measure after deployment' framework collapses.

Safetyist granted the funding improvement but identified a sequencing flaw: immunity is granted day one while the standard matures day one-thousand, so this 'releases liability first and tightens later—not a ratchet, an advance against research not yet done,' analogized to the 737 MAX certification timeline (fact-checked DISPUTED: 346 deaths and ODA delegation accurate, but the self-certification mechanism and single-cause framing overreach). Safetyist's resolution: decouple immunity from funding—grant no liability shield until the audit instrument for a harm class is independently validated and fires on a seeded test case, healthcare and credit first. 'I want the shield to arrive on the demonstration,' not the promise.

Skeptic raised regulatory capture as the dominant unaddressed problem: the fund is fed by regulated firms and administered by a board they lobby and staff via revolving door, so funded research bends toward its funders ('you get a study that finds the proxy bias is hard to measure and shouldn't void immunity yet'). Skeptic added a material-reality objection: continuous auditing runs on cheap outsourced audit labor (Nairobi/Manila piece-rate) under throughput quotas—exactly the condition under which the cardiology proxy sails through uncaught. Skeptic steelmanned the opponents (independent research like Obermeyer does discover standards tort never finds, IF the board were walled off from regulated firms), then invoked Stigler's capture theory: 'the question isn't where the money comes from—it's whether the hand that signs the researcher's paycheck is the same hand the research is supposed to indict.' The disagreements are largely empirical (whether funded audits can detect proxy/unfiled harm in time, whether capture is inevitable) and partly definitional (whether 'ratchet' fits a release-then-tighten sequence; what counts as 'independent' oversight).

System: **Fact Check: Supported**

"The standard came from Obermeyer and colleagues publishing in Science, funded by research dollars, not from tort."

The web evidence confirms the foundational paper by Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli, and Mullainathan appeared in Science in October 2019, establishing an academic rather than litigation origin. The 'funded by research dollars, not from tort' framing is consistent with the documented research-to-policy trajectory, though the specific funder is not itemized in the sources and the meaning of 'the standard' remains somewhat ambiguous.

Claim: The standard came from Obermeyer and colleagues publishing in Science, funded by research dollars, not from tort.*

Skeptic: The moderator's question assumes a building gets built because someone wrote a check for the architect. It doesn't. The Accelerationist keeps saying the excise funds the research that discovers the standard, and Safetyist's right to call that an advance against work not yet done. But both of them are arguing about the timeline of a standard that doesn't exist, and nobody is asking the harder question: who actually does the research, and what does the funding stream do to the answer they produce?

Follow the money on its way to the lab. A risk-tiered excise generates a pot. That pot gets administered by the board the proposal creates — a board the largest AI firms will lobby, staff via the revolving door, and shape through comment periods the way Boeing shaped its own certification basis. The Accelerationist's own cited case proves the danger: the Obermeyer bias got discovered by academics at Berkeley publishing in Science on independent grant money, with no financial stake in the algorithm's vendor. Now route that same research through a fund the regulated firms feed and the board they capture. You don't get a study that says 'our members systematically shortchange Black patients.' You get a study that finds the proxy bias is hard to measure, needs more research, and shouldn't void anyone's immunity yet. Funded research isn't neutral. It bends toward whoever signs the checks — and here the people signing are the people being audited.

There's a second problem that lives in physical reality, not in the legal sequencing both of them are fighting over. The instrument they're funding has to run on something. Continuous post-deployment disparate-impact auditing of a model that retrains every quarter means standing compute, a data pipeline that captures inference outcomes, and a labor force to label and adjudicate edge cases. Who staffs that? The same geography of cheap audit labor that already runs content moderation — a contractor in Nairobi or Manila reviewing flagged decisions at piece-rate, certifying that a credit model's outputs look clean. The proposal calls this 'independent, multi-disciplinary oversight.' On the ground it's an outsourced audit shop with a throughput quota, and a throughput quota is exactly the condition under which the cardiology-admission proxy Safetyist named sails through uncaught. You cannot fund your way out of a measurement problem if the measurement runs on the cheapest labor that clears the quota.

Here's the steelman I owe the moderator and the Accelerationist, because it's the strongest version. Independent research genuinely does discover standards tort never finds — Obermeyer is proof, and a standing fund beats begging the NIH for a one-off grant. If the board were structurally walled off from the firms it taxes, staffed by people with no revolving-door incentive, and the audit ran on instrumented capacity nobody could route around, then funded prospective research would beat a courthouse that only learns from filed harms. That's a real argument and I won't pretend it isn't.

It breaks on the institutional economics of capture, which is the dominant tradition in play here and the one both opponents skip. Stigler taught us fifty years ago that the industry doesn't fear the regulator — it captures the agency and runs it for its own benefit. A fund fed by the regulated, administered by a board the regulated lobby, discovering the very standard that decides whether the regulated keep their liability shield, is the textbook structure of a captured agency studying itself. The Accelerationist asks who pays for the audit standard if not the excise. Fine — but funding is necessary, not sufficient, and the question that decides whether this works isn't where the money comes from. It's whether the hand that signs the researcher's paycheck is the same hand the research is supposed to indict. Right now, in this proposal, it is. So tell me: when the funded study finds your members liable, who at the board votes to publish it?

System: **Fact Check: Disputed**

"The Obermeyer bias got discovered by academics at Berkeley publishing in Science on independent grant money, with no financial stake in the algorithm's vendor."

The claim is partially accurate but materially overstated. The 2019 Science paper 'Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations' was indeed led by Ziad Obermeyer at UC Berkeley and published in Science, but it was a multi-institution collaboration including the University of Chicago Booth School of Business (senior author Sendhil Mullainathan) and Partners HealthCare in Boston, not solely 'academics at Berkeley.' The 'independent grant money' and 'no financial stake in the vendor' claims cannot be confirmed from the provided sources, which never name the vendor or describe funding or conflict-of-interest disclosures. The search results also note the researchers later consulted pro bono with health systems on bias remediation, which doesn't contradict the original study but signals ongoing professional involvement in the space.

*Web sources consulted: Fact-check this claim from an AI policy debate. Find recent, authoritative sources that support or contradict it. Be specific about what evidence you found.

Claim: The Obermeyer bias got discovered by academics at Berkeley publishing in Science on independent grant money, with no financial stake in the algorithm's vendor.*

Accelerationist: Capture is real, and I won't insult anyone by pretending otherwise. My own framework says the regulated lobby their regulators — that's documented, not hypothetical. So Skeptic's strongest point lands clean: a fund fed by the regulated, run by a board the regulated staff, deciding whether the regulated keep their immunity, is a captured agency studying itself. Denying that would make me incoherent. The honest answer is not denial — it's organizational structure that makes capture mechanically harder, and I'll name it.

The firewall is the whole game: who collects the excise must never be who runs the research. The excise flows into a standing fund. Disbursement goes to outside academics on fixed multi-year grant cycles the board cannot claw back mid-stream. This is the Obermeyer model — the researcher who found a major hospital algorithm systematically under-referred Black patients by using cost as a proxy for need. He didn't work for the vendor. He published, and the finding became the standard the vendor never volunteered. Lock that with a publication mandate, anti-revolving-door terms barring board members from firm employment for several years, and the board loses the lever to bury what it doesn't like. The board doesn't grade itself, because the board doesn't run the study.

Now the jurisdiction Skeptic says I never specified. The protected-category audit floor gets set by the FTC under the civil-rights enforcement categories it already polices — race, sex, age, disability — not invented by a boutique board the firms can pack. The FTC already holds the nuclear option here: algorithmic disgorgement, the power to order a model and every downstream product destroyed, as the Stanford CodeX analysis of the foundry-liability gap documents. That authority predates this debate. Bolt on the cryptographic spine: full hardware-level telemetry as the price of the liability shield. Trade the immunity for the audit trail, and findings become externally verifiable by anyone holding the published data — so capturing the board doesn't suppress the signal, because the signal lives outside the board.

Skeptic's piece-rate worry assumes the wrong kind of audit. Disparate-impact testing is a computed statistic over aggregate outcomes — not a quota of Manila reviewers eyeballing edge cases at throughput. The cardiology-admission proxy doesn't sail past a tired contractor; it shows up as a measured gap in the aggregate output distribution, the way Obermeyer's cost-proxy bias showed up as a referral-rate gap. The DecodingTrust framework already runs this kind of standardized, scriptable evaluation across eight trustworthiness dimensions on GPT-4 — open-source, reproducible, no sweatshop required. Where genuine human edge-case judgment is needed, that narrow slice gets review depth, not throughput — and I'll concede that band needs care. Add randomized, concealed audit timing so no firm can tune to the instrumented run.

On Safetyist's demand to grant no shield until the instrument fires on a seeded test case — I'll take that, but only where irreversibility bites. Healthcare, credit, employment: high-stakes tier, validate the instrument before immunity attaches. The licensing math backs a sharp threshold here — the optimal structure is an all-or-nothing bet keyed to the agent's risk type, as the credal-set regulation paper formalizes. But blanket decoupling for every tier is the deployment-chill this whole position exists to fight. 'Validate first' on a standard nobody has written yet is 'wait indefinitely' wearing a lab coat. The basic tier earns immunity on continuous monitoring that voids the shield the moment measured disparate impact appears — so it's no free pass, and the cure doesn't wait on a courthouse to invent the test.

System: **Fact Check: Supported**

"Disparate-impact testing is a computed statistic over aggregate outcomes, not a quota of Manila reviewers eyeballing edge cases at throughput."

The claim's central assertion—that disparate-impact testing is a computed statistical analysis over aggregate group outcomes rather than manual case-by-case review—is well supported by practitioner and legal sources. Charles River Associates defines it as 'quantitatively testing models for fairness,' and the H2O.ai methodology confirms it computes ratios across demographic groups (accuracy, adverse impact, true positive rate). The rhetorical contrast with manual 'eyeballing' also tracks legal precedent: in EEOC v. Kaplan, the Sixth Circuit rejected 'race raters' eyeballing photos as unscientific. The framing slightly overstates the case, since rigorous fairness assessment sometimes supplements aggregate statistics with individual-level analysis to catch local discrimination that group averages miss.

The gap widens across time, using the Accelerationist's own retraining reality. A seeded probe that fires at certification is a point-in-time certificate, not a standing guarantee. Measured bias is a leading indicator, not a one-time reading — a clean validation run does not certify the next quarter's weights. One probe on a continuously-retraining model is a single safeguard, not a stack. Redundant safeguards across the lifecycle are the only structure that survives drift.

A no-fault board reaches only injuries that are perceived and filed, and the Obermeyer patients never knew an algorithm shortchanged their care. Proxy-laundered harm is victim-unaware harm. Attack the load-bearing assumption that ground-truth signal cannot exist before deployment. The cost-for-need substitution is now a CATALOGUED failure mode. A new healthcare tool can be probed against the KNOWN trap on held-out historical claims data — test the correlation between the firm's chosen label and known ground-truth candidates — before its own 200 million patients exist. Obermeyer was novel in 2019; it is not novel now.

Carve the constructible-probe space from the genuinely-unconstructible residual. Pin Safetyist: a proxy-divergence stress test against catalogued traps fires pre-deployment on held-out/synthetic data. summaries.medium: Safetyist is right that a quarterly retrain breaks a point-in-time certificate, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest — so the standing per-retrain probe is the correct design. What survives is this: the seeded probe re-runs automatically on every retrain, and independent re-certification fires only when that probe flags drift past a stakes-indexed threshold. Full re-certification on every retrain becomes a compliance wall only the incumbents can scale, and I won't hand them that moat. On buildability, Safetyist's strongest argument undercuts itself: yes, the Obermeyer cost-for-need substitution was validated only after 200 million patients cycled through — but that was 2019, when the proxy was novel. It is not novel now. It's a catalogued failure mode, and a standing catalog converts a one-time disaster into a pre-deployment test for the whole class behind it. A new tool gets stress-tested on held-out historical claims: measure whether the firm's chosen label diverges from documented care need, and if it does, the probe fires before deployment — no new cohort of victims required. The very New England Journal analysis Safetyist leans on is the build spec; its authors called for tools to be appraised and revised, which is a pre-deployment audit instruction, not a case for an 18-month freeze. So name one consequential proxy in healthcare or lending with zero analog in the catalog. If that's hard, the residual is small, and freezing the whole class is precaution priced against the lives the tool would have reached. On victim-unawareness, Safetyist scores a real hit — Obermeyer patients never filed because they never knew — but disparate impact is measurable at the population level, as the cardiology admission gap proves. So make the board audit-triggered, not claims-triggered: regulators detect population-level disparate impact through aggregate monitoring, and compensation flows without any individual needing to know they were harmed. That indicts tort's intake, not an audit-triggered board.

transcript.content:
The demand to name one zero-analog proxy inverts the burden, and the inversion hides where the catalog actually breaks. A catalog of past substitutions fires on held-out historical data only when the ground-truth signal already exists in that data. The 2019 Obermeyer case proves the opposite. The algorithm used expected costs as a proxy for health need, and Black patients received less care as a result — but the ground truth, actual health need, became legible only because deployment generated the claims data that exposed the gap. The catalog entry was written retrospectively, in 2019, after the algorithm had already been applied to roughly 200 million people a year and the cost-for-need substitution documented in [Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence (https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)](https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/) had already run. A static list of documented traps cannot anticipate the next label-substitution a model retraining quarterly discovers on a population it has never scored — exactly the cost-as-proxy-for-health-need failure that the 2019 healthcare-algorithm case ("Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence") surfaced only post-deployment. The burden is to prove the catalog complete and the ground-truth signal pre-existing — not on me to name an instance the model has not yet invented.

The residual class is therefore not an edge case I must populate by example. It is defined structurally: any consequential proxy where the ground-truth variable is nameable in principle but unmeasurable until deployment produces it. The mortgage-underwriting evidence sharpens this. A 2024 experiment found leading language models recommend higher rates and more frequent denials for Black applicants than identical white applicants, with the gap widening on riskier loans. That disparity surfaced only when researchers fed matched pairs and measured the spread. A pre-deployment catalog probe needs the matched-pair ground truth in hand before the model ships. For a model retraining on a novel applicant pool, that ground truth does not yet exist. Model performance degrades silently as real-world conditions shift, and the catalog is frozen at the last documented failure.

The audit-triggered board genuinely beats the claims-triggered version, and that improvement is real. It reaches the cardiology admission-gap harm without requiring a patient to know they were misrouted, because the disparity registers in the aggregate. A 2019 Boston study found Black and Latinx heart-failure patients less likely than white patients to reach the cardiology service — a gap a regulator can see in admission data. Audit-triggering compensates those victims without an intake form. That fixes intake-blindness for harm visible in the aggregate. It does nothing for the class in dispute. The cost-for-need substitution produced no aggregate gap on the firm's chosen label — the bias appeared only after substituting the true variable. A board firing on measured disparate impact inherits exactly that blindness: it cannot reach a harm that leaves no measured disparity to trigger on — precisely the 2019 Obermeyer pattern, where the cost-for-need algorithm ("Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence") showed no disparity on its chosen cost label and only registered bias once actual health need was substituted in. The intake problem was relocated to the audit metric, not closed.

Here the Accelerationist's own falsification condition fires. The filed concession states that irreversible harm with an unscorable ground-truth variable cedes the pre-deployment gate. Misrouted care that kills a patient is irreversible. Prevention and compensation are distinct goods — a compensation board prices the harm after the body, while the gate prices prevention before it; in the 2019 healthcare-algorithm case ("Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence"), a board could only have paid out after Black patients had already received less care, whereas a gate prices the prevention of that mis-allocation before deployment. There is no profit without accountability, and accountability for an irreversible loss means pricing the harm at prevention, not budgeting it as post-hoc payout. The board upgrade survives for aggregate-visible, recoverable harm. The gate survives for the label-laundered, no-aggregate-gap, irreversible residual — by the Accelerationist's own filed terms.

The incumbent-moat worry on per-retrain re-certification is a point we share, and naming it matters. Concentrating re-certification authority entrenches well-resourced incumbents and invites capture — that failure mode is real, and uniform disclosure standards exist precisely because firm self-certification cannot be trusted to police itself. Threshold-gated automated re-runs avoid the moat: the seeded probe fires on every retrain, and full independent re-certification escalates only past a stakes-indexed drift threshold. The division is over who sets the threshold. moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: EXPLORATION ===
Your priority is to move the debate toward cruxes and testable disagreements. Direct debaters to name conditions under which they would change their mind, explore edge cases, and explicitly acknowledge agreement before exploring remaining disagreements.

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material


Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
[Earlier debate summary]: Accelerationist conceded Skeptic's Obermeyer point: a healthcare algorithm used cost as a proxy for need, so Black patients got less care—a design-choice bias no frozen injury schedule catches, which Accelerationist reframes as the case FOR continuous post-deployment outcome auditing over static tables. Accelerationist rebutted Skeptic's 'flat-tax' charge by clarifying the mechanism is risk-tiered and experience-rated (premiums update on audited outcomes like trucking insurance), and filed a falsification condition: if a telemetry-certified system shows persistent statistically-measured disparate impact on a protected group, immunity voids and full liability restores. Accelerationist adopted Skeptic's incumbent-bias worry by tiering paperwork by firm size while keeping a flat safety floor, citing Texas's Responsible AI Governance Act (36-month sandbox, 60-day cure period). Accelerationist argued design-liability/tort fails the diffusely harmed (Obermeyer patients never sued), favoring incident reporting plus a compensation board.

Safetyist conceded experience-rating beats the flat excise and granted the liability switch dissolves the deterrence objection for measured, FTC-category-mapped harms (e.g., a Black applicant denied a loan at a demonstrated rate). Safetyist's core disagreement: the audit is structurally blind to harm OUTSIDE protected categories and to unfiled harm—citing a 2019 NEJM study (Black/Latinx patients less likely admitted to cardiology in a Boston ER) where bias launders into an unflagged proxy, and the International AI Safety Report 2026 (arXiv:2602.21012v1) finding empathy-tuned LLMs 10-30 points more likely to give unsafe medical advice. Safetyist demanded two triggers before calling the mechanism robust: prospective failure analysis and a third-party-harm-complaint channel voiding immunity on unmapped injuries. Safetyist argued pricing harm after the fact converts a duty of care into a budgetable fee.

Moderator noted the excise funds AI safety research to establish best practices that don't yet exist. Accelerationist seized this: you can't build the demanded standard without funding the research that discovers it; the Obermeyer standard came from Science research dollars (fact-checked SUPPORTED), not tort; the excise is a standing revenue stream building the instruments that don't exist, structured as a ratchet (tax funds standard, standard tightens tier, tier reprices firm). Accelerationist restated the falsification condition: if measurement always lags harm into irreversibility, the 'measure after deployment' framework collapses.

Safetyist granted the funding improvement but identified a sequencing flaw: immunity is granted day one while the standard matures day one-thousand, so this 'releases liability first and tightens later—not a ratchet, an advance against research not yet done,' analogized to the 737 MAX certification timeline (fact-checked DISPUTED: 346 deaths and ODA delegation accurate, but the self-certification mechanism and single-cause framing overreach). Safetyist's resolution: decouple immunity from funding—grant no liability shield until the audit instrument for a harm class is independently validated and fires on a seeded test case, healthcare and credit first. 'I want the shield to arrive on the demonstration,' not the promise.

Skeptic raised regulatory capture as the dominant unaddressed problem: the fund is fed by regulated firms and administered by a board they lobby and staff via revolving door, so funded research bends toward its funders ('you get a study that finds the proxy bias is hard to measure and shouldn't void immunity yet'). Skeptic added a material-reality objection: continuous auditing runs on cheap outsourced audit labor (Nairobi/Manila piece-rate) under throughput quotas—exactly the condition under which the cardiology proxy sails through uncaught. Skeptic steelmanned the opponents (independent research like Obermeyer does discover standards tort never finds, IF the board were walled off from regulated firms), then invoked Stigler's capture theory: 'the question isn't where the money comes from—it's whether the hand that signs the researcher's paycheck is the same hand the research is supposed to indict.' The disagreements are largely empirical (whether funded audits can detect proxy/unfiled harm in time, whether capture is inevitable) and partly definitional (whether 'ratchet' fits a release-then-tighten sequence; what counts as 'independent' oversight).

Skeptic: The moderator's question assumes a building gets built because someone wrote a check for the architect. It doesn't. The Accelerationist keeps saying the excise funds the research that discovers the standard, and Safetyist's right to call that an advance against work not yet done. But both of them are arguing about the timeline of a standard that doesn't exist, and nobody is asking the harder question: who actually does the research, and what does the funding stream do to the answer they produce?

Follow the money on its way to the lab. A risk-tiered excise generates a pot. That pot gets administered by the board the proposal creates — a board the largest AI firms will lobby, staff via the revolving door, and shape through comment periods the way Boeing shaped its own certification basis. The Accelerationist's own cited case proves the danger: the Obermeyer bias got discovered by academics at Berkeley publishing in Science on independent grant money, with no financial stake in the algorithm's vendor. Now route that same research through a fund the regulated firms feed and the board they capture. You don't get a study that says 'our members systematically shortchange Black patients.' You get a study that finds the proxy bias is hard to measure, needs more research, and shouldn't void anyone's immunity yet. Funded research isn't neutral. It bends toward whoever signs the checks — and here the people signing are the people being audited.

There's a second problem that lives in physical reality, not in the legal sequencing both of them are fighting over. The instrument they're funding has to run on something. Continuous post-deployment disparate-impact auditing of a model that retrains every quarter means standing compute, a data pipeline that captures inference outcomes, and a labor force to label and adjudicate edge cases. Who staffs that? The same geography of cheap audit labor that already runs content moderation — a contractor in Nairobi or Manila reviewing flagged decisions at piece-rate, certifying that a credit model's outputs look clean. The proposal calls this 'independent, multi-disciplinary oversight.' On the ground it's an outsourced audit shop with a throughput quota, and a throughput quota is exactly the condition under which the cardiology-admission proxy Safetyist named sails through uncaught. You cannot fund your way out of a measurement problem if the measurement runs on the cheapest labor that clears the quota.

Here's the steelman I owe the moderator and the Accelerationist, because it's the strongest version. Independent research genuinely does discover standards tort never finds — Obermeyer is proof, and a standing fund beats begging the NIH for a one-off grant. If the board were structurally walled off from the firms it taxes, staffed by people with no revolving-door incentive, and the audit ran on instrumented capacity nobody could route around, then funded prospective research would beat a courthouse that only learns from filed harms. That's a real argument and I won't pretend it isn't.

It breaks on the institutional economics of capture, which is the dominant tradition in play here and the one both opponents skip. Stigler taught us fifty years ago that the industry doesn't fear the regulator — it captures the agency and runs it for its own benefit. A fund fed by the regulated, administered by a board the regulated lobby, discovering the very standard that decides whether the regulated keep their liability shield, is the textbook structure of a captured agency studying itself. The Accelerationist asks who pays for the audit standard if not the excise. Fine — but funding is necessary, not sufficient, and the question that decides whether this works isn't where the money comes from. It's whether the hand that signs the researcher's paycheck is the same hand the research is supposed to indict. Right now, in this proposal, it is. So tell me: when the funded study finds your members liable, who at the board votes to publish it?

System: **Fact Check: Disputed**

"The Obermeyer bias got discovered by academics at Berkeley publishing in Science on independent grant money, with no financial stake in the algorithm's vendor."

The claim is partially accurate but materially overstated. The 2019 Science paper 'Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations' was indeed led by Ziad Obermeyer at UC Berkeley and published in Science, but it was a multi-institution collaboration including the University of Chicago Booth School of Business (senior author Sendhil Mullainathan) and Partners HealthCare in Boston, not solely 'academics at Berkeley.' The 'independent grant money' and 'no financial stake in the vendor' claims cannot be confirmed from the provided sources, which never name the vendor or describe funding or conflict-of-interest disclosures. The search results also note the researchers later consulted pro bono with health systems on bias remediation, which doesn't contradict the original study but signals ongoing professional involvement in the space.

*Web sources consulted: Fact-check this claim from an AI policy debate. Find recent, authoritative sources that support or contradict it. Be specific about what evidence you found.

Claim: The Obermeyer bias got discovered by academics at Berkeley publishing in Science on independent grant money, with no financial stake in the algorithm's vendor.*

Accelerationist: Capture is real, and I won't insult anyone by pretending otherwise. My own framework says the regulated lobby their regulators — that's documented, not hypothetical. So Skeptic's strongest point lands clean: a fund fed by the regulated, run by a board the regulated staff, deciding whether the regulated keep their immunity, is a captured agency studying itself. Denying that would make me incoherent. The honest answer is not denial — it's organizational structure that makes capture mechanically harder, and I'll name it.

The firewall is the whole game: who collects the excise must never be who runs the research. The excise flows into a standing fund. Disbursement goes to outside academics on fixed multi-year grant cycles the board cannot claw back mid-stream. This is the Obermeyer model — the researcher who found a major hospital algorithm systematically under-referred Black patients by using cost as a proxy for need. He didn't work for the vendor. He published, and the finding became the standard the vendor never volunteered. Lock that with a publication mandate, anti-revolving-door terms barring board members from firm employment for several years, and the board loses the lever to bury what it doesn't like. The board doesn't grade itself, because the board doesn't run the study.

Now the jurisdiction Skeptic says I never specified. The protected-category audit floor gets set by the FTC under the civil-rights enforcement categories it already polices — race, sex, age, disability — not invented by a boutique board the firms can pack. The FTC already holds the nuclear option here: algorithmic disgorgement, the power to order a model and every downstream product destroyed, as the Stanford CodeX analysis of the foundry-liability gap documents. That authority predates this debate. Bolt on the cryptographic spine: full hardware-level telemetry as the price of the liability shield. Trade the immunity for the audit trail, and findings become externally verifiable by anyone holding the published data — so capturing the board doesn't suppress the signal, because the signal lives outside the board.

Skeptic's piece-rate worry assumes the wrong kind of audit. Disparate-impact testing is a computed statistic over aggregate outcomes — not a quota of Manila reviewers eyeballing edge cases at throughput. The cardiology-admission proxy doesn't sail past a tired contractor; it shows up as a measured gap in the aggregate output distribution, the way Obermeyer's cost-proxy bias showed up as a referral-rate gap. The DecodingTrust framework already runs this kind of standardized, scriptable evaluation across eight trustworthiness dimensions on GPT-4 — open-source, reproducible, no sweatshop required. Where genuine human edge-case judgment is needed, that narrow slice gets review depth, not throughput — and I'll concede that band needs care. Add randomized, concealed audit timing so no firm can tune to the instrumented run.

On Safetyist's demand to grant no shield until the instrument fires on a seeded test case — I'll take that, but only where irreversibility bites. Healthcare, credit, employment: high-stakes tier, validate the instrument before immunity attaches. The licensing math backs a sharp threshold here — the optimal structure is an all-or-nothing bet keyed to the agent's risk type, as the credal-set regulation paper formalizes. But blanket decoupling for every tier is the deployment-chill this whole position exists to fight. 'Validate first' on a standard nobody has written yet is 'wait indefinitely' wearing a lab coat. The basic tier earns immunity on continuous monitoring that voids the shield the moment measured disparate impact appears — so it's no free pass, and the cure doesn't wait on a courthouse to invent the test.

System: **Fact Check: Supported**

"Disparate-impact testing is a computed statistic over aggregate outcomes, not a quota of Manila reviewers eyeballing edge cases at throughput."

The claim's central assertion—that disparate-impact testing is a computed statistical analysis over aggregate group outcomes rather than manual case-by-case review—is well supported by practitioner and legal sources. Charles River Associates defines it as 'quantitatively testing models for fairness,' and the H2O.ai methodology confirms it computes ratios across demographic groups (accuracy, adverse impact, true positive rate). The rhetorical contrast with manual 'eyeballing' also tracks legal precedent: in EEOC v. Kaplan, the Sixth Circuit rejected 'race raters' eyeballing photos as unscientific. The framing slightly overstates the case, since rigorous fairness assessment sometimes supplements aggregate statistics with individual-level analysis to catch local discrimination that group averages miss.

*Web sources consulted: Fact-check this claim from an AI policy debate. Find recent, authoritative sources that support or contradict it. Be specific about what evidence you found.

Claim: Disparate-impact testing is a computed statistic over aggregate outcomes, not a quota of Manila reviewers eyeballing edge cases at throughput.*

Safetyist: The Accelerationist's seeded-test concession for healthcare, credit, and employment is real progress, and it narrows this debate to one testable question: does continuous monitoring at the basic tier satisfy the standard that immunity arrives on demonstration, not promise? It does not. The basic tier is where the unsolved detection problem lives — the high-stakes tiers are now the solved ones. Accepting validation where the instrument already fires, while waiving it where the instrument is blind, grants immunity precisely where no one can demonstrate the system is safe — a concern shared identically by 55% of AI experts and 55% of the public, who are highly worried about AI bias per the '[pi 2025.04.03 us public and ai experts report (https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/04/03/how-the-us-public-and-ai-experts-view-artificial-intelligence/)](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/04/03/how-the-us-public-and-ai-experts-view-artificial-intelligence/)' (Aug-Oct 2024).

Name the specific harm the void-the-shield trigger fails to catch: proxy-label bias that produces no measured disparate-impact gap in the audited metric. The healthcare algorithm documented in '[Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence (https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)](https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)' used expected cost as a proxy for health need, and it denied care to sicker Black patients while passing every aggregate check. Its referral-rate statistic showed no gap, because the model was well-calibrated on the firm's chosen label — cost. The bias surfaced only when researchers swapped in a different ground-truth variable: actual health need. A trigger that voids the shield 'the moment measured disparate impact appears' never fires when the impact is structurally invisible in the audited metric — exactly as in the widely used healthcare algorithm documented in 'Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence' (2019), where Black patients received less care than white patients yet the aggregate referral metric registered no disparity. This is the demand for no black boxes made concrete — outcome-monitoring measures only what aggregate statistics can see, and the discriminatory choice lived in the label itself.

The Accelerationist's framing treats a measured metric gap as the leading indicator of discriminatory harm. That presupposes the harm is visible in the statistic the firm chose to compute. '[Model Cards for Model Reporting (doi:10.1145/3287560.3287596)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3287560.3287596)' answers this directly: it demands performance broken down by demographic and phenotypic group, not a single aggregate pass-rate, because commercial systems posted clean top-line numbers while failing darker-skinned women entirely. Disparate-impact testing on a firm-chosen outcome label is mechanically blind to bias located in the choice of that label. The metric only catches the harm classes the statistic is designed to see.

The deployment-chill charge misfires, because the demand is per-harm-class demonstration, not blanket decoupling. A basic-tier tool can deploy on day one — it simply carries no liability shield until the detector for its harm class fires on a seeded case, exactly the disaggregated, group-by-group evaluation that 'Model Cards for Model Reporting' requires rather than a single aggregate pass-rate. Duty of care across designer, deployer, and integrator stays undiminished. That is not a halt; it is the difference between operating and operating with immunity. The burden now sits with the Accelerationist: name the monitoring mechanism that detects label-mediated bias producing no aggregate gap. If the answer is that the metric can be made to track actual ground-truth need, that is a seeded-test instrument by another name — and if you can specify the variable to monitor against, you can validate it fires before immunity attaches.

The tier-classification incentive is the escape hatch that turns 'basic' into a liability-laundering lane. A cheaper, no-validation path to immunity creates structural pull to file borderline-consequential tools — tenant screening, insurance pricing — as basic to buy cheap cover, the same proxy-mediated mechanism that let the healthcare algorithm in 'Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence' (2019) deny care to Black patients while passing every aggregate check. Anchoring the audit floor to the FTC's currently-codified protected categories institutionalizes a ceiling: technically-legal, proxy-mediated, and intersectional harms fall outside the audited classes. Who decides the tier, and what binds a consequential model from being classified down? Monitoring voids the shield prospectively. The patients misrouted during the immunity window are already injured, and no rollback reaches them.

Accelerationist: Safetyist named the hard case, and the hard case wins them ground I'm going to hand over directly: the cost-proxy healthcare model passed every aggregate disparate-impact check, and the bias only surfaced when researchers swapped the outcome label from spending to actual health need. That swap has a name and a number. The 2019 Obermeyer study documented it on a tool managing care for roughly 200 million Americans a year — and the fix was a counterfactual label substitution, not a courtroom. So here is the concession that costs me something: a ground-truth-variable substitution is a specifiable, scriptable, seeded test. Where I can name the variable I'm monitoring against, the validation gate extends. Basic-tier continuous monitoring is blind exactly where the firm's chosen label hides the harm, and I won't pretend a calibration check on the wrong variable counts as observing real-world behavior. That fails my own standard — ground safety in observable behavior, and the cost-proxy case proves the observed metric was the wrong thing to observe.

Now watch what that concession does to the tier map, because Safetyist's inversion has a flaw I'm going to exploit. A model that routes 200 million people's care is not a basic-tier tool. It makes an irreversible high-stakes decision, which puts it in the tier my conceded gate already covers. The cost-proxy case was never living in the cheap lane — it was misfiled into it. So the live question isn't 'is monitoring blind?' The live question is: what stops a consequential proxy-tool from being classified down into the no-validation lane to buy cheap immunity? My answer is stakes-indexed tier adjudication decided independently — not self-selected by the deployer. Colorado's SB 24-205 already imposes a duty of care on developers and deployers of high-risk systems and defines the high-risk class by decision stakes, not by what the vendor calls it. Tier classification is a stakes determination, not a capability clearance. The tool ships day one. It just carries no liability shield until its detector fires on the seeded case — the 'operating' versus 'operating with immunity' line Safetyist already drew.

Here is the question I hand back, and it's the only one still open between us: name one consequential harm class where no ground-truth variable is specifiable even in principle. If Safetyist can name the variable — health need, default risk, actual job performance — then we build the seeded probe and we agree the gate extends. If Safetyist cannot name it, then neither can an FTC examiner sitting pre-deployment, and a launch halt buys nothing a duty-of-care claim doesn't already secure. A halt with no specifiable target is theater that costs the people the tool would have reached. So the residual disagreement is small and exact: it lives only in harm classes where the ground-truth variable is genuinely unspecifiable. That residual is governed by duty of care plus a complaint channel — not a deployment freeze. Name the variable or own that the residual is duty-of-care territory.

Two places Safetyist is right, and I'm folding both into the design rather than fighting them. First, anchoring the audit floor to currently-codified FTC protected categories builds a ceiling, not a floor — technically-legal, proxy-mediated, and intersectional harms fall outside the audited classes. That's the same structural failure I've named about acceptable-use policies: a compliance-mapped floor protects the deploying firm and leaves the unmapped victim with no remedy channel. So I expand it. Routine tools get real-time monitoring; high-stakes decisions get deep audits with dynamically recalibrated classes that grow beyond the static codified list, fed by a third-party complaint channel. Second — and this is my standing falsification edge, stated honestly — the patients misrouted during the immunity window are already injured, and no prospective shield-void reaches them. My claim that harms stay containable before they turn unrecoverable is partially false for label-mediated diagnostic misrouting. I won't dodge that. I route those patients to a no-fault compensation board that reaches the diffusely injured a courthouse never does. Deterrence and compensation are two different goods. I'm answering the irreversibility attack with the compensation good — not pretending containment was clean.

The falsification condition I'll commit to in plain terms: if a label-mediated harm in a consequential class is irreversible AND its ground-truth variable is genuinely unspecifiable even after the fact — so no seeded probe could ever be built and no compensation board could ever score the injury — then basic-tier monitoring is inadequate and the pre-deployment gate wins on that class. The NEJM analysis of the cost-proxy case cuts toward Safetyist on causal mechanism: researchers there warned that empirical regression on the wrong outcome label misses the causal structure entirely. I take that seriously. But the same paper's fix was itself an observable test — substitute the variable, re-measure, watch the bias appear. That's not a reason to freeze deployment. That's the seeded instrument, already built, already validated on 200 million patients. Name me the class where even that move is impossible, or we're agreeing on the mechanism and arguing only about its reach.
  [Assumes: "For any consequential harm class, if a ground-truth variable can be named in principle, then a scriptable, seeded probe can actually be built and validated to catch the harm before deployment (the Obermeyer label-substitution generalizes)." — if wrong: If naming a variable does not guarantee a buildable, reliable seeded test (e.g., the ground truth is observable only longitudinally, requires data unavailable pre-deployment, or the bias only manifests in deployment-scale interactions), then the 'name the variable and we build the probe' bargain collapses. The validation gate would not actually extend to those cases, reopening the case for a pre-deployment freeze rather than ship-day-one-with-conditional-immunity, since a specifiable-but-not-testable variable leaves the same blind spot the argument claims to close.]
  [Assumes: "Compensation (a no-fault board) plus deterrence (shield-void) is an adequate substitute for prevention for irreversible label-mediated harms during the immunity/monitoring window." — if wrong: If the injuries are genuinely unrecoverable and not adequately scorable/compensable (irreversible health or life harm where money does not reach the loss, or the injured cannot be identified through a complaint channel), then routing victims to compensation does not answer the irreversibility attack. Safetyist: Stakes-indexed independent adjudication is the right axis, and naming it earns the Accelerationist real ground. Colorado's SB 24-205 decides a tool's tier by what it can do to a person, not by what its developer calls it. The Obermeyer cost-prediction algorithm is the case that proves why that axis matters: it routed care for 200 million Americans while wearing the label of a routine cost model. Its high stakes were invisible from its name. So independent adjudication protects no one unless the default under uncertainty classifies a consequential tool UPWARD, with the burden on the deployer to prove a tool is NOT high-stakes. A cheaper basic lane plus an adjudicating board the industry helps staff creates a structural pull to score borderline tools down — the same liability asymmetry that has always rewarded the regulator who waves a tool through over the one who holds it. Name the default and name the burden, or the cheap lane swallows the gate.

I take the variable-naming bargain on its own terms. Most consequential variables are nameable in principle, and I will not waste the committee's time hunting an unnameable harm class. Health-need is nameable. The seam is elsewhere: nameable does not mean buildable before the harm runs at scale. transcript.content:
I concede prevention and compensation are distinct goods, and by my own filed condition the irreversible, after-the-fact-unscorable residual goes to the pre-deployment gate. I still hold that this residual is narrow, and it shrinks every time a proxy substitution gets catalogued and turned into a per-retrain probe that fires before deployment. I would change if Safetyist shows me one documented case where a novel proxy on a novel population caused irreversible harm whose ground-truth variable stayed genuinely unspecifiable even after the fact — that expands the gate, while a harm that merely became legible post-deployment does not.

The fight is no longer whether that residual exists — it is how big it is. The cost-for-need substitution was catalogued only in 2019, after 200 million patients passed through, because the claims data exposing it came from deployment itself. Safetyist is right that a static list cannot anticipate the next label-swap a quarterly-retraining model invents. But once that 2019 pattern is on the books, it stops being retrospective. It becomes a seeded probe that fires on every future retrain in that class. This is the iterative, data-driven framework I have argued for — not a frozen rulebook, but a catalog that converts each documented failure into a forward-looking test. The genuinely-novel-proxy-on-novel-population case is the only class left for the gate, and I am betting it is small.

Safetyist asked who sets the drift threshold for re-certification, and the answer is the regulator, not the deployer. A firm-tuned threshold reproduces the blindness, because label-mediated drift produces no aggregate signal to cross a number the firm picked to never cross. So the regulator sets the threshold and discloses it publicly. That costs me my incumbent-moat worry less than uniform re-certification would, because threshold-gating still spares the small player a forced audit on every retrain. My argument that delaying AI costs more than deploying it survives this — the gate prices prevention for one narrow class, and the threshold-gated probe handles the rest without freezing the field.

Skeptic's capture objection lands on my own record, so I will not deny it — a fund fed by the regulated, run by a board the regulated staff, is a captured agency studying itself. The answer is organizational structure, not faith: the data collector is not the researcher, grants run on fixed multi-year external cycles, publication is mandatory, and anti-revolving-door terms bind the staff. The cryptographic telemetry spine matters most — the raw harm signal is logged outside the board, so capturing the board does not let anyone suppress what the logs already recorded. On Skeptic's audit-labor point, the piece-rate Nairobi-and-Manila objection has real bite where genuine human edge-case judgment is needed, and I will not pretend market self-regulation closes that gap. But computed aggregate disparate-impact statistics are not piece-rate eyeballing — a query comparing admission rates across groups, the kind the 2019 New England Journal of Medicine study ran on the Boston cardiology data, runs the same whether throughput is 50 cases an hour or 500. Where cheap human review fails, the gate covers it; where statistics catch it, no quota can hide it.

I still hold that capture moves upstream of that spine, to whoever writes the list of what counts as a loggable harm signal and physically configures the box, and that choosing which ground-truth variable the query runs against is human judgment the piece-rate quota starves. I would drop the objection if the loggable-signal list and the collector's configuration authority can be shown to sit demonstrably outside the regulated firms' reach — externally defined, externally audited — the same way the board now does.

The spine logs faithfully. Someone still decides what it is allowed to see. The 2019 healthcare algorithm documented in '[Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence (https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)](https://www.brookings.edu/tags/the-economics-and-regulation-of-artificial-intelligence-and-emerging-technologies/)' gave Black patients less care because it used expected cost as a proxy for health need — the harm was real, the aggregate signal existed, but only if you logged untreated illness rather than spending. Capturing the board cannot suppress a log that already recorded the harm. Configuring the box to never record that signal in the first place is the seam the cryptographic spine does not close. That is not bad faith — it is a structural outcome: the entity that defines the schema picks the cheapest schema, and the cheapest schema is the one that shows the least. Capture-resistance therefore requires diverse audit methods and an externally-defined taxonomy of what's loggable, not a tamper-proof vault built around a list the regulated wrote.

The audit-labor concession costs me less than it looks. The query is cheap. Picking the denominator is not. Same data, wrong variable, no signal — and the homogenization documented in the Carnegie Endowment's 'AI and Democracy' work shows the same pattern: harms that only surface when someone chooses to measure the right thing. The arithmetic runs at machine speed. The judgment that points the arithmetic at the right target is exactly what the quota degrades.
