Skeptic is right about where the capture went, and the reason I know they're right is that they just described my own argument back to me. I've said for three rounds that acceptable-use policies protect the platform from liability, not the user from harm. The entity that defines which signals get logged reproduces that exact seam — it picks the cheapest schema, logs dollars spent instead of illness left untreated, and the cryptographic spine records that lie faithfully forever. So the answer can't be market self-regulation. A firm that writes its own loggable-harm list writes itself a clean record. The fix is structural: schema authority sits outside the regulated, or it's worthless. I'll name the body, since nobody answered when I named it before — the FTC's existing civil-rights impact categories already define protected-class disparate-impact variables, they were built outside the AI firms, and they carry enforcement teeth under existing statute. My acceptance of this entire framework is conditional on that. External body holds the schema, or there's no deal.

The denominator problem splits cleanly, and pretending it doesn't is how both sides have talked past each other. Picking which ground-truth variable to run the query against is human judgment. A piece-rate quota starves it — same data, wrong variable, no signal, Skeptic nailed that. But once the variable is chosen, the disparate-impact arithmetic runs identically at 50 cases an hour or 500. So automate the part that's arithmetic and route the part that's judgment to the external body. Variable selection is an organizational-design question about who holds authority, not a throughput question about how fast an agent computes. The FTC civil-rights categories pick the denominator. The automated query runs it at machine speed. That's not a contradiction in automating compliance — it's the line automation actually draws.

Safetyist's per-class seeded test is the iterative, data-driven framework I've been demanding since round one, so I'll take it. A gate that fires on a demonstration and clears on a demonstration is a trigger, not a freeze. Healthcare and credit first, threshold-gated re-runs on retrain, the regulator setting and publicly disclosing the drift threshold — that's exactly the evolving framework that replaces static rules. The medical case in the [Failure Modes in Machine Learning (arXiv:1810.07339)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.07339) corpus shows why the residual is real: an 8% data-poisoning rate shifted anticoagulant dosage by 75% for half the patients, and that's irreversible the moment the dose goes in. A seeded test that probes for that before deployment is cheap insurance against an injury you can't refund. I'll take the bounded exit-conditioned gate over the catastrophic backlash that an uncaught harm triggers — because the harsher freeze that comes after a scandal is the real threat to long-run deployment speed.

Here's the residual I still contest, and it's the only one left. My own falsification condition already cedes the gate for harm that's irreversible and unscorable even after the fact. Fine. But that class shrinks every time a proxy substitution gets catalogued into a per-retrain probe — that's the whole point of building an evolving catalog of failure modes. The over 200 adversarial-ML papers published between February 2024 and February 2026 are 200 proxy patterns converted from unknown to testable. So expanding the gate past the residual now carries a burden: name a documented case of irreversible harm whose ground-truth variable stayed unspecifiable even after the fact. That's an empirical bet, not a values gap. We agree on the gate's shape. We disagree on how often the world hands us a harm nobody can ever score. Bring the case that settles it, or the gate stays narrow.

The asymmetric cost of delay survives intact for everything outside that residual — and that's almost everything. Delaying the deployable, scorable, catalogued majority still costs lives we could reach. The gate only earns its keep on the genuinely unscorable sliver. So I'll sign the deal: external FTC schema authority, the per-class seeded exit, the narrow residual gate. The remaining fight is a falsifiable wager about catalog completeness, and I'm betting the catalog closes faster than the residual grows.

key_assumptions.assumption: An external body (the FTC's civil-rights impact categories) can hold schema authority over which harm signals get logged, and those pre-existing categories are adequate, enforceable, and outside the capture of the regulated firms.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If the FTC categories are themselves capturable, under-resourced, miss harm types specific to AI deployment, or lack real enforcement teeth, then the structural fix collapses. The whole conditional acceptance ('External body holds the schema, or there's no deal') voids, and the argument reverts to its own objection: a firm writing its own clean record. The deal he signs becomes unsignable.

key_assumptions.assumption: Variable selection (denominator/judgment) cleanly separates from the disparate-impact arithmetic (throughput/computation), so judgment can be routed to the external body while the rest is safely automated at machine speed.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If denominator choice is entangled with the computation (e.g., new data distributions, edge cases, or runtime conditions require ongoing human judgment about which variable applies), then automation re-imports the very judgment he tried to externalize. The 'line automation actually draws' blurs, and his concession that high-throughput automation is safe for the arithmetic portion no longer holds.

key_assumptions.assumption: The catalog of documented failure modes / proxy patterns closes faster than the residual class of irreversible, permanently-unscorable harms grows — and the opponent cannot produce a case of such harm.
key_assumptions.if_wrong: If novel irreversible harms emerge faster than they can be catalogued, or even one documented case of permanently-unscorable irreversible harm exists, his 'empirical bet' is lost. ## Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms
★ [sit-176] Claims-Driven Liability Mechanisms Are Blind to Unlitigated Harms: A situation in which liability tools that price off realized, attributed, and litigated harm fail to deter injuries that are never perceived, filed, or recoverable. Encompasses: experience-rated premiums priced off filed claims, the loss-history loop's dependence on litigation, diffuse small-dollar harms (e.g., loan denials or biased screens) that no plaintiff pursues, victims unable to perceive the AI decision that injured them, and catastrophic tail damages exceeding any bond or capitalization floor.
  Your interpretation: A conceded limit of market-based deterrence: experience-rated premiums, capitalized shells, and tort recovery act as a 'faster discount window, not deterrence' because the most common harms never enter the pricing engine. Names the failure mode absent from prior nodes asserting market-based deterrence, without conceding that all AI harm is invisible or that public enforcement is the only channel.
  Safetyist: Evidence that a capitalization floor answers solvency and an insurer answers payment, but neither answers deterrence for harm that is never litigated. Reinforced by survey data showing many subjects do not know an AI decision affected them, leaving diffuse and catastrophic harms outside the loss loop. Distinct from attribution within a layered chain and from pricing risk through liability.

missing_arguments.argument: The Noise Thesis cuts in favor of acceleration: because Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein show human professionals like radiologists and judges produce wildly inconsistent decisions on identical cases, every month an AI deployment is delayed by liability fear leaves patients exposed to the documented harm of noisy human judgment. Deploying flawed-but-auditable AI now beats waiting for perfect AI while noisy humans keep injuring people.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It directly operationalizes the framework's own cited research into an affirmative deployment-speed argument that the synthesis never converted into a concrete cost-of-delay claim.

missing_arguments.argument: An excise tax funding a compensation board creates a moral-hazard fiscal trap because the fund's solvency depends on the very deployment volume it is supposed to make safe, so regulators will face structural pressure to keep tiers cheap and approve risky models to keep revenue flowing. The 9/11 Victim Compensation Fund and Superfund both ran dry and required repeated bailouts, and a self-funded AI board will face the same insolvency spiral when a single large-scale model failure generates mass claims.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It identifies a self-undermining incentive baked into the funding mechanism with two concrete federal precedents of compensation funds going insolvent.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: Unlimited tort liability collapsed the U.S. childhood vaccine supply in the 1980s, and the 1986 VICP no-fault fund rebuilt the supply while paying injured families faster than litigation — paying over $5 billion since.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that asks whether a no-fault administrative compensation fund modeled on VICP can simultaneously stabilize the supply of a beneficial-but-risky technology and deliver faster victim compensation than tort litigation. Encompasses: liability-induced supply collapse, administrative compensation funds, faster-than-litigation victim payment, the historical VICP precedent. Excludes: experience-rating tax design, capture of the administrative board, generic liability-allocation across the AI lifecycle.

accelerationist.belief: Unlimited tort exposure demonstrably froze a life-saving product market until a liability shield restored it, proving liability is the binding constraint on beneficial deployment.
accelerationist.desire: To remove the liability chill so socially valuable AI reaches users at maximum rate.
accelerationist.intention: Cite VICP as proof-of-concept that immunity-plus-fund unlocks supply, then transplant the structure wholesale to AI developers.
accelerationist.summary: VICP proves a liability shield is the unlock for stalled beneficial technology.

safetyist.belief: VICP shows a no-fault fund can compensate injured parties reliably without requiring victims to prove fault against asymmetrically powerful defendants.
safetyist.desire: To guarantee injured people are actually made whole rather than abandoned by an adversarial tort system.
safetyist.intention: Adopt the no-fault fund but condition the immunity it buys on verified adherence to safety standards, so the shield is earned not granted.
safetyist.summary: VICP is a victim-protection mechanism worth replicating only if coupled to safety conditions.

skeptic.belief: The VICP analogy holds only for the narrow facts of a homogeneous, well-characterized product with a small injury taxonomy, and the $5B figure reflects decades of a bounded harm space.
skeptic.desire: To avoid importing a precedent whose fit to heterogeneous, opaque AI harms is assumed rather than demonstrated.
skeptic.intention: Accept the historical fact while interrogating whether AI's unbounded and label-mediated harms can be administered like a vaccine injury table.
skeptic.summary: VICP worked for bounded vaccine harms; its transfer to open-ended AI harms is unproven.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: The historical claim is shared but each POV reads a different lesson: unlock (acc), victim protection (saf), analogy fragility (skp). No existing node captures the no-fault-fund-as-supply-stabilizer framing; 'The Tort System's Natural Adaptation Cycle' is adjacent but is about courts adapting, not about a statutory fund replacing tort.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: A flat excise tax prices admission rather than marginal harm; experience-rating (premiums that update on audited outcomes) is the superior mechanism because it reprices the firm that produces measured harm.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns whether liability or tax instruments should reprice each firm dynamically based on its own audited harm record rather than charging a flat entry fee. Encompasses: experience-rated premiums, marginal-harm pricing, outcome-conditioned tax updating, the flat-fee critique. Excludes: how the harm metric itself is defined or audited, capture of the rate-setting body, the existence of the fund per se.

accelerationist.belief: A flat tax penalizes all entrants equally and dampens deployment, whereas experience-rating leaves safe high-volume deployers cheap and only taxes actual measured harm.
accelerationist.desire: To minimize the deadweight cost on beneficial low-harm deployment while still funding the system.
accelerationist.intention: Push experience-rating so compliant fast-movers pay less, accelerating safe adoption rather than taxing admission flatly.
accelerationist.summary: Experience-rating keeps safe deployment cheap and only prices actual harm.

safetyist.belief: Premiums that update on audited outcomes create a continuous financial gradient toward safer behavior, unlike a one-time flat fee with no marginal incentive.
safetyist.desire: To make firms internalize the safety consequences of their own deployments on an ongoing basis.
safetyist.intention: Tie premium updates to audited harm so the cost of carelessness rises with each measured failure.
safetyist.summary: Experience-rating builds a live financial incentive to reduce real harm.

skeptic.belief: A flat tax merely prices admission and lets repeat-harm firms pay a fixed toll, so only outcome-indexed pricing tracks the actual distribution of damage.
skeptic.desire: To prevent the program from becoming a flat 'license to harm' purchased once and forgotten.
skeptic.intention: Demand experience-rating while flagging that it depends entirely on a trustworthy harm measurement it cannot itself supply.
skeptic.summary: Flat fees are a license to harm; experience-rating is necessary but only as good as its metrics.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Shared preference for experience-rating over flat tax, but acc wants cheapness for safe firms, saf wants behavioral gradient, skp wants to block a flat license-to-harm. Related existing nodes ('Business Skin in the Game', 'Normal Externality Management', 'Mileage Fee as Internalization Mechanism') touch internalization but none specifically captures the flat-vs-experience-rated repricing dispute. Not a clean map.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: The Obermeyer 2019 cost-as-proxy-for-need healthcare algorithm systematically under-referred Black patients and would pass aggregate telemetry checks, because the bias lived in the firm's chosen label rather than any audited metric.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_label: Label Choice as the Locus of Hidden Bias
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns harms arising from a firm's choice of proxy label (e.g., cost as a stand-in for need) that aggregate performance telemetry cannot detect because the metric itself encodes the bias. Encompasses: proxy-label bias, telemetry-invisible discrimination, the Obermeyer case, audit blindness to upstream target definition. Excludes: aggregate-vs-subgroup performance failures that audited metrics could catch, drift over time, malicious adversarial attacks.

accelerationist.belief: The bias was a discrete upstream design error in label selection, fixable by correcting the target variable rather than by abandoning algorithmic decision-making.
accelerationist.desire: To preserve auditable AI's noise-reduction advantage by treating label bias as a correctable engineering fault, not a reason to halt deployment.
accelerationist.intention: Concede the Obermeyer failure while arguing telemetry plus label-review fixes it, keeping the case for AI over noisy human judgment intact.
accelerationist.summary: Obermeyer was a correctable label bug, not an indictment of auditable AI.

safetyist.belief: Because the bias lived in the chosen label, no aggregate audit metric would ever flag it, exposing a structural blind spot in any telemetry-only compliance regime.
safetyist.desire: To ensure the safety regime can catch harms that hide upstream of the metrics it monitors.
safetyist.intention: Use Obermeyer to justify mandatory scrutiny of label and target-variable choices, not just output telemetry.
safetyist.summary: Obermeyer proves telemetry-only audits are blind to label-encoded harm.

skeptic.belief: A widely deployed algorithm caused systematic racial under-referral and passed every aggregate check, showing compliance theater cannot substitute for understanding the firm's modeling choices.
skeptic.desire: To prevent a NAIICP from certifying harmful systems as 'safe' merely because they clear audited metrics.
skeptic.intention: Wield Obermeyer as evidence that the proposed audit infrastructure will systematically miss the very harms it claims to govern.
skeptic.summary: Obermeyer shows audited compliance can certify harm as safe.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Existing nodes 'When AI Works on Average but Fails Specific Groups' and 'Model-Dependent Racial Disparity Heterogeneity' are close, but those concern subgroup performance gaps detectable in principle; this agreement is specifically about bias hidden in the target-label choice that aggregate telemetry cannot see. The 'Optimizing for Narrow Metrics vs. Real-World Goals' node is also adjacent but generic. The label-locus framing is distinct enough to warrant a new node.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: The regulated-funded, revolving-door board is a genuine capture risk, and the answer is structural: separate the data collector from the researcher, fixed multi-year external grant cycles, mandatory publication, anti-revolving-door terms, and a cryptographic telemetry spine logging raw signals outside the board.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_label: Structural Capture-Proofing of the Oversight Board
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns designing the institutional structure of an industry-funded AI oversight body to resist regulatory capture through separation of functions, term limits, mandatory publication, and tamper-evident logging held outside the body. Encompasses: revolving-door risk, collector-researcher separation, external grant cycles, cryptographic telemetry spine as anti-capture infrastructure. Excludes: the substantive safety standards the board enforces, drift thresholds, the tax mechanism funding it.

accelerationist.belief: Capture would equally let a board be weaponized to block competitors, so structural independence protects deployers from arbitrary or rival-driven gatekeeping.
accelerationist.desire: To keep the board from becoming a discretionary chokepoint that throttles deployment.
accelerationist.intention: Back structural safeguards and an external cryptographic log so compliance is rule-bound and predictable rather than captured by any faction.
accelerationist.summary: Structural independence prevents the board from becoming a deployment chokepoint.

safetyist.belief: An industry-funded board with a revolving door will predictably soften standards unless its functions are split and its raw data sits beyond its control.
safetyist.desire: To guarantee the safety regime cannot be quietly hollowed out by the firms it polices.
safetyist.intention: Hard-wire collector-researcher separation, anti-revolving-door terms, and an externally held telemetry spine to preserve enforcement integrity.
safetyist.summary: Only structural separation keeps an industry-funded board from softening safety.

skeptic.belief: Regulator-funded-by-the-regulated bodies historically drift toward capture regardless of intentions, so trust must be replaced by externally verifiable structure.
skeptic.desire: To avoid a 'governance mirage' where a captured board legitimizes harm under a veneer of oversight.
skeptic.intention: Insist that raw signals be logged cryptographically outside the board so capture leaves a verifiable trail, treating the board itself as untrustworthy by default.
skeptic.summary: Assume capture by default and externalize the evidence so it cannot be buried.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Existing nodes 'Governance Mirage', 'Swivel Chair Governance', and 'Privatization of Proof' are thematically adjacent but none specifically addresses the structural anti-capture design (collector-researcher separation + external cryptographic spine) of an industry-funded board. Warrants a distinct node.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: The drift threshold for re-certification must be set and publicly disclosed by the regulator, not the deployer, because a firm-tuned threshold reproduces metric-blindness for label-mediated drift that produces no aggregate signal.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns who sets and discloses the quantitative threshold at which model drift triggers re-certification, contending that deployer-tuned thresholds reproduce blind spots while regulator-set, publicly disclosed thresholds resist gaming. Encompasses: drift threshold authorship, public disclosure of thresholds, gaming via self-set thresholds, label-mediated drift invisibility. Excludes: the re-certification escalation mechanism itself, capture of the board, the underlying label-bias problem in static models.

accelerationist.belief: A single publicly disclosed regulator threshold gives every firm a clear, stable target instead of bespoke negotiated thresholds that breed uncertainty.
accelerationist.desire: To get predictable, uniform re-certification triggers that don't impose ad hoc deployment delays.
accelerationist.intention: Support a transparent regulator-set threshold as a bright-line rule that reduces compliance ambiguity for fast iteration.
accelerationist.summary: A public regulator threshold gives firms a predictable bright line.

safetyist.belief: A deployer-tuned threshold will be set to avoid triggering scrutiny, so only an independently set threshold can reliably catch dangerous drift.
safetyist.desire: To ensure drift that endangers people actually forces re-certification rather than being defined away.
safetyist.intention: Mandate regulator authorship and disclosure of the threshold so firms cannot calibrate it to evade review.
safetyist.summary: Independent thresholds prevent firms from defining away dangerous drift.

skeptic.belief: Firm-set thresholds reproduce the same metric-blindness as the Obermeyer label problem, since label-mediated drift produces no aggregate signal a self-interested firm would surface.
skeptic.desire: To stop the program from outsourcing its own evidentiary standard to the party with the strongest incentive to game it.
skeptic.intention: Require public regulator-set thresholds as a precondition, while noting even disclosed thresholds may miss signal-free drift.
skeptic.summary: Self-set thresholds recreate metric-blindness; disclosure is necessary but insufficient.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Existing nodes 'Benchmark Saturation and Metric Decay', 'Latent Entropy Divergence as System Metric', and 'Supervisability Evasion' touch metric drift and evasion, but none addresses the governance question of who authors and discloses the drift threshold. Distinct enough to be new.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: Per-retrain re-certification by an independent body would build an incumbent moat only large firms could clear; the workable design is automated seeded probes re-running on every retrain with full independent re-certification escalating only past a stakes-indexed drift threshold.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns avoiding an incumbent-favoring re-certification burden by using cheap automated seeded probes on every retrain and reserving costly full independent re-certification for cases exceeding a stakes-indexed drift threshold. Encompasses: automated seeded probes, stakes-indexed escalation, incumbent-moat avoidance in compliance design, per-retrain monitoring. Excludes: who sets the drift threshold, the firm-size tiering of telemetry burden generally, the substantive safety floor.

accelerationist.belief: Mandatory full re-certification per retrain would freeze iteration and hand incumbents a moat, while automated probes let small firms ship updates fast.
accelerationist.desire: To preserve rapid iteration and low barriers to entry for smaller deployers.
accelerationist.intention: Push automated probes as the default and reserve expensive human re-certification for genuinely high-stakes drift to keep deployment velocity high.
accelerationist.summary: Automated probes keep iteration fast and avoid an incumbent moat.

safetyist.belief: Continuous automated probes on every retrain catch more drift more often than periodic heavyweight reviews, while escalation preserves rigor where stakes are highest.
safetyist.desire: To maintain genuine safety coverage across all retrains without gaps between expensive reviews.
safetyist.intention: Endorse always-on probes plus stakes-indexed escalation so safety scales with risk rather than with firm size.
safetyist.summary: Always-on probes plus risk-indexed escalation keeps coverage continuous.

skeptic.belief: A per-retrain full-re-certification rule would entrench only the firms able to absorb its cost, concentrating the market and the harm.
skeptic.desire: To prevent compliance design from becoming an unintended consolidation tool that protects incumbents.
skeptic.intention: Support automated probes while watching whether the stakes-index is itself gamed to keep escalation rare.
skeptic.summary: Avoid a re-certification rule that consolidates the market behind incumbents.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Related to 'Regulatory Fragmentation and Cost Burden' and 'Automated Compliance Monitoring' and 'Audit Replay Capability', but those are generic; the specific incumbent-moat-avoidance-via-seeded-probes-with-stakes-indexed-escalation design is not captured. New node justified.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: Heavy telemetry compliance burden can crush small developers and entrench incumbents, so administrative burden should be tiered by firm size while keeping the substantive safety floor and duty of care undiminished.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_label: Size-Tiered Burden with Undiminished Safety Floor
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns scaling administrative/telemetry compliance burden by firm size to avoid entrenching incumbents while holding the substantive safety floor and duty of care constant across all firms. Encompasses: firm-size-tiered administrative burden, incumbent entrenchment via compliance cost, the distinction between procedural burden and substantive safety floor. Excludes: re-certification escalation mechanics, drift-threshold authorship, the tax rate structure itself.

accelerationist.belief: Uniform heavy telemetry requirements impose fixed costs that small developers cannot absorb, killing competition and innovation at the bottom of the market.
accelerationist.desire: To keep entry barriers low so a competitive ecosystem of small AI developers can flourish.
accelerationist.intention: Advocate lighter procedural burden for small firms to maximize the number of viable deployers and the pace of innovation.
accelerationist.summary: Tier procedural burden down so small developers can compete and innovate.

safetyist.belief: Procedural burden and the substantive safety floor are separable, so administrative load can be lightened for small firms without lowering the actual duty of care owed to users.
safetyist.desire: To ensure every user receives the same safety protection regardless of which firm deployed the system.
safetyist.intention: Tier only paperwork and telemetry overhead while holding the safety floor and duty of care identical for all firms.
safetyist.summary: Lighten paperwork for small firms but never the safety floor itself.

skeptic.belief: A flat heavy compliance regime functions as a barrier to entry that incumbents can weaponize, concentrating both market power and the capacity to cause harm.
skeptic.desire: To prevent the safety regime from being captured as an anti-competitive moat dressed up as safety.
skeptic.intention: Back size-tiered burden while scrutinizing whether 'small firm' carve-outs become loopholes that erode the floor in practice.
skeptic.summary: Tier burden to block compliance-as-moat, but guard against carve-out loopholes.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Closely related to existing 'Regulatory Fragmentation and Cost Burden' and 'Regulatory Arbitrage via Externalization', but the specific claim — tier *administrative burden* by size while holding the *substantive safety floor* constant — is a distinct design principle separating procedure from substance. Distinct from the automated-probes node (agreement 6) which is about re-certification mechanics. New node justified.
